name: Proxies
intent: Place an intermediary between clients and servers that can hide, protect, speed up or control the traffic passing through it, either on the client's side (forward proxy) or the server's side (reverse proxy).
scenario: A company wants employees' web access filtered and logged, and also wants its public website to be fast and protected from attacks, without changing the application behind it.
problem: Direct connections expose both ends: servers are reachable by anyone, clients reveal their addresses and cannot be filtered, and every server must do its own encryption, compression, caching and attack defence. An intermediary can do this work once, in one place, so that the application behind it stays simple.

howItWorks.title: A forward proxy acts for the client
howItWorks.text: Clients send requests to the proxy, which makes them to the internet on their behalf. The destination sees the proxy's address, not the client's. Organisations use forward proxies to filter and log outgoing traffic, cache downloads and enforce policy; privacy services use them to hide the client.

howItWorks.title: A reverse proxy acts for the server
howItWorks.text: Clients believe they talk to the site, but the reverse proxy receives the request and forwards it to one of the servers behind it. The servers' real addresses stay hidden, and the proxy is the single public entry point. Nginx, HAProxy, Envoy and cloud load balancers are reverse proxies.

howItWorks.title: What a reverse proxy typically does
howItWorks.text: It terminates TLS (decrypts HTTPS at the proxy) so backends do plain HTTP, compresses responses, caches static and cacheable content, balances load across servers, retries or fails over when a backend is down, rate limits and filters malicious requests (a web application firewall), and adds logging and headers such as the original client address.

howItWorks.title: The proxy sees everything, so it must be trusted and passed through
howItWorks.text: Because the backend sees the proxy as the client, the real client address must be passed in a header such as X-Forwarded-For, and the backend must trust that header only when it comes from the proxy. Traffic between the proxy and the backends should stay on a private network or be re-encrypted.

howItWorks.title: A proxy is also a risk and a bottleneck
howItWorks.text: Every request passes through it, so it must be fast, stateless where possible and run as several instances. A misconfiguration affects everything behind it. Layering proxies (CDN, gateway, sidecar) adds latency and makes failures harder to trace.

pros: Hides servers and clients, and gives one place to enforce policy
Offloads TLS, compression and caching from the application
Enables load balancing, failover and gradual rollouts behind one address
Adds logging and metrics without changing the application
cons: An extra hop adds a little latency
A single point of failure unless it is run redundantly
Real client addresses are lost unless forwarded and trusted correctly
Hard to debug when several proxies are chained
whenToUse: Reverse proxy in front of almost every production web service
Forward proxy for corporate egress (outgoing traffic) control, filtering and caching
Whenever several backends should look like one service
whenNotToUse: A tiny internal service with one trusted caller, where a proxy adds a hop for no benefit
As a place for business logic: keep it to networking concerns
pitfalls: Trusting X-Forwarded-For from anyone, which lets clients fake their address
Caching responses that are private to a user, and serving them to others
Running a single proxy instance and making it the weakest link
Leaving backend servers directly reachable, which bypasses the proxy's protections

roles.label: Proxy
roles.description: Sits in the middle and applies its features.

quiz.question: A hospital wants to block staff from file-sharing sites and log all outbound web requests. Separately, it wants its patient portal to sit behind one public entry point that hides the application servers. Which setup fits?
options: A reverse proxy for both, since both sit between users and servers
A forward proxy for both, since both filter and log requests
Forward proxy for staff traffic, reverse proxy in front of the portal
A reverse proxy for staff traffic and a forward proxy for the portal
quiz.explanation: A forward proxy acts for the clients and controls what they reach. A reverse proxy acts for the servers and is the single public face. Mixing them up would filter the wrong direction of traffic.

quiz.question: An app sits behind nginx and rate limits by the first IP in the X-Forwarded-For header. An attacker sends a different made-up X-Forwarded-For value with every request and never hits the limit. What is the right fix?
options: Rate limit by the connecting socket address, which is always the real client
Trust the header only from the proxy and use the address the proxy added
Encrypt the hop between nginx and the app with TLS so the header cannot be forged
Strip X-Forwarded-For everywhere and ignore client addresses completely
quiz.explanation: Clients can send any header, so a value is trustworthy only if the proxy set or appended it. The socket address behind a proxy is the proxy itself, so limiting on it throttles everyone together. TLS on that hop does not stop the client from sending a fake header.

quiz.question: A reverse proxy caches GET /account responses for 60 seconds, keyed on the URL alone. The response includes the signed-in user's name and address. Users start seeing other people's details. Which change fixes the cause?
options: Lower the cache lifetime to 5 seconds so that far fewer users are affected by it
Add a second proxy layer so requests are spread over more caches
Turn on compression so the cached bodies are harder to read
Mark per-user responses Cache-Control: private so shared caches never store them
quiz.explanation: A shared cache with a key that ignores the user hands one user's private page to the next. A shorter TTL (cache lifetime) still leaks, only less often. The response must be marked as not cacheable by shared caches, or the cache key must include the user.
